facts.statement: Convolosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Aptian age.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous, Aptian

facts.statement: Convolosaurus lived in North America approximately 125 million years ago during the middle Cretaceous.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace 125 millones de años, durante el Aptiense en lo que es hoy Norteamérica

facts.statement: The name Convolosaurus means "flocking lizard" because fossils were found in a dense concentration at Proctor Lake in Texas.
facts.quote: Convolosaurus (, meaning "flocking lizard" after the concentration of juvenile fossils found) is a genus of basal ornithopod dinosaur from the Twin Mountains Formation from Proctor Lake in Comanche County, Texas.

facts.statement: James "Rusty" Branch discovered the fossil site in May 1985, noting it was one of the richest Lower Cretaceous sites in North America.
facts.quote: In May 1985, James "Rusty" Branch at the Proctor Lake in Comanche County, Texas, discovered a dinosaur fossil site which was among the richest from the Lower Cretaceous of North America.

facts.statement: The discovery of the site was reported in the scientific literature in 1988.
facts.quote: The discovery was in 1988 reported in the scientific literature.

facts.statement: The species Convolosaurus marri was formally named and described in 2019 by Kate A. Andrzejewski, Dale A. Winkler, and Louis Leo Jacobs.
facts.quote: In 2019, the type species Convolosaurus marri was named and described by Kate A. Andrzejewski, Dale A. Winkler and Louis Leo Jacobs.

facts.statement: The genus name comes from the Latin word for "to flock," referring to the high density of fossils found at the site.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Latin convolare, "to flock", a reference to the dense concentration of fossils.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is a partial skeleton including a skull found in the Aptian-aged Twin Mountains Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype, SMU 72834, was found in a layer of the Twin Mountains Formation dating from the Aptian. It consists of a partial skeleton with skull.

facts.statement: The holotype individual was a subadult.
facts.quote: It represents a subadult individual.

facts.statement: The holotype individual was estimated to be between 2.5 and 3 meters long.
facts.quote: The holotype individual had an estimated length of between 2.5 and 3 m.

facts.statement: Because the holotype was not fully grown, the adult size of Convolosaurus remains unknown.
facts.quote: It was not yet fully grown, so the adult size was considered to be unknown.

facts.statement: A unique trait of Convolosaurus is that the premaxilla bears four teeth with a vertical trough on the outside.
facts.quote: The premaxilla bears four teeth, which have a vertical trough on the outside.

facts.statement: The neck vertebrae are opisthocoelous, meaning they are convex at the front and concave at the rear.
facts.quote: The neck vertebrae are opisthocoelous, convex at the front and concave at the rear.

facts.statement: Convolosaurus is classified as a basal ornithopod dinosaur, positioned between Hypsilophodon and Thescelosaurus in the evolutionary tree.
facts.quote: While initially considered a member of the Hypsilophodontidae, Convolosaurus was in 2019 placed in the Ornithopoda in a basal position, between Hypsilophodon and Thescelosaurus in the evolutionary tree.

facts.statement: The placement of Convolosaurus reversed previous views because it shares two supraorbitals with Thescelosaurus, suggesting Hypsilophodon lost this trait independently.
facts.quote: Previous analyses had found Thescelosaurus to be more basal than Hypsilophodon but this was now reversed as Convolosaurus possessed two supraorbitals that it shared with Thescelosaurus, indicating that Hypsilophodon had lost this trait independently.

facts.statement: Although initially thought to be a member of Hypsilophodontidae, Convolosaurus was classified in 2019 as a basal ornithopod above Hypsilophodon and below Thescelosaurus.
facts.quote: Aunque inicialmente se consideraba un miembro de Hypsilophodontidae, Convolosaurus fue clasificado en 2019 en Ornithopoda en una posición basal, por encima de Hypsilophodon y por debajo de Thescelosaurus en el árbol evolutivo.

facts.statement: Fossils from the site have been combined into three mounted skeletons displayed at the Proctor Lake US Army Corps of Engineers Office, the Perot Museum of Nature and Science, and the Fort Worth Museum of Science and History.
facts.quote: Remains found were combined into three mounted skeletons displayed at respectively the Proctor Lake US Army Corps of Engineers Office at Proctor (based on specimen SMU 70456), the Perot Museum of Nature and Science, (a composite of specimens SMU 74087, SMU 74093 and SMU 74104), and the Fort Worth Museum of Science and History (based on specimen SMU 74663).

facts.statement: The genus Convolosaurus was described by Andrzejewski and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: Andrzejewski et al. 2019

facts.statement: Convolosaurus belongs to the family Tenontosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Tenontosauridae

facts.statement: Convolosaurus is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Convolosaurus lived during the Aptian stage, between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (119.57 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Convolosaurus has been recorded so far.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1

rejected.quote: In 2019 these amounted to 488 specimens, representing at least twenty-nine individuals, ranging from small juveniles to subadults.
